transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Date: 2026-03-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Crestline Head of ML), Evan Li (Crestline Platform Eng), Jordan Price (Crestline CTO)

SUMMARY (auto-generated, may be rough): Discussed p95 latency targets for customer-facing chat, concurrency needs for batch and streaming use cases, options between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, benchmarking plan (token/sec), and next steps to run an initial pilot and share SOC2/security docs.

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, this is Marco, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:06] Aisha Khan: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to get into this.
[00:00:10] Jordan Price: Hi all. We'll be focused on latency and throughput today — we've got realtime chat and long-form generation workloads.
[00:00:20] Marco Diaz: Great. Quick agenda: understand Crestline's SLOs (p95), concurrency, streaming behavior; run through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs; and agree next steps for benchmarking.
[00:00:30] Evan Li: Sound good. I'll ask the infra questions.

[00:01:05] Aisha Khan: To give context: customer-facing chat for payments — a mix of short Q&A and longer reconciliation reports. Targets: p95 latency for short responses 300-500ms, for longer messages up to 2s-3s. Concurrency: typical active concurrent users ~120, but could spike to 600 during peak campaign. Streaming is important — we stream partial responses to the client.
[00:01:40] Lena Park: Thanks, that's helpful. When you say p95 300-500ms, is that end-to-end client-to-client or just token generation time?
[00:01:48] Aisha Khan: End-to-end from request to first token on the client. We do some preprocessing client-side, but we want first token under 500ms for short prompts.
[00:01:58] Marco Diaz: Good distinction. For Redwood Hosted we usually quote server-side p95 generation time; network round-trip depends on region. We can route to nearest region and measure.

[00:02:30] Jordan Price: We're also comparing tradeoffs of Hosted vs Dedicated: cost predictability and isolation for Dedicated are attractive, but we'd like to know if Hosted can meet our p95 numbers without going Dedicated right away.
[00:02:42] Lena Park: Right — Hosted is fastest to start, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and guaranteed throughput. For p95 under 500ms for short prompts, it depends on model size, batch settings, and whether you use streaming optimizations and prefix caching.

[00:03:15] Evan Li: Can you give ballpark tokens/sec per GPU for the 2 model families we mentioned in the NDA — the smaller efficient chat model and the larger assistant model?
[00:03:24] Marco Diaz: Ballpark: on a modern A100-ish or equivalent, a 7B family model with optimized kernels/quantization can do ~2-3k tokens/sec for generation workloads with continuous batching; a 70B-ish model is more like 500-1200 tokens/sec depending on kv-cache and sequence length. But these are approximate — real numbers vary based on prompt length and top-p settings.
[00:03:52] Aisha Khan: Okay that aligns with internal estimates. For our short prompts average generation is 20-40 tokens; longer reports are 800-1,500 tokens. That long tail worries us for latency and cost.

[00:04:15] Marco Diaz: For short prompts the first-token latency is often dominated by model startup and scheduling. Redwood uses continuous batching and KV cache to reduce repeated context overhead. Also streaming lowers perceived latency since first tokens are sent immediately while later tokens follow.
[00:04:34] Lena Park: We should also think about concurrency vs throughput. If you have 120 active users with an average of 20 tokens each at the same time, that's 2.4k tokens in-flight. If spike to 600, that's 12k tokens in-flight. The system needs enough capacity so p95 stays comfortable.

[00:05:10] Jordan Price: What's your usual approach to calculate required GPU count for Dedicated?
[00:05:16] Marco Diaz: We start with tokens/sec requirements, add headroom (burst factor) and map to measured tokens/sec per GPU for your model variant. For example, if your steady-state is 5k tokens/sec and one GPU is 2.5k tokens/sec, you'd need 2 GPUs, but we'd advise 3-4 to handle bursts and autoscaling latency.
[00:05:34] Evan Li: How fast is autoscaling on Dedicated? If we get a sudden spike, will we see a p95 spike for a minute?
[00:05:41] Lena Park: Dedicated supports horizontal scaling with configurable burst capacity. There is some provisioning time, but we have warm pool options and burst capacity to cover short spikes. Still, spikes can cause temporary p95 increases unless you provision warm capacity.

[00:06:10] Aisha Khan: We want to avoid p95 regressions during spikes — can you route requests to a smaller, cheaper model as fallback?
[00:06:17] Marco Diaz: Yes, smart routing/fallback policies are supported: route by latency or cost. You can configure a fallback to a lower-latency variant when load is high. Logging and tracing will show fallbacks so you can evaluate quality impact.

[00:06:45] Jordan Price: Security is also a must — VPC/private deployment options and KMS for keys. Are audit logs and SSO included?
[00:06:53] Lena Park: For Hosted we have SOC 2, SSO, RBAC, and key management integrations. Private deployments (VPC or on-prem) give you tenant isolation and you manage networking. We'll share our security pack after the call.

[00:07:22] Evan Li: Network latency from our users is another variable; we're US east and europe. Does Redwood provide regional routing?
[00:07:29] Marco Diaz: Yes, Hosted supports region routing. Dedicated can be region-specific. For strict data residency we'd look at Private deployments.

[00:07:50] Aisha Khan: Back to benchmarks — what's the recommended test plan to validate p95 and tokens/sec?
[00:07:57] Marco Diaz: We usually ask for a representative prompt set (short, mid, long, streaming), target concurrency pattern, and desired p95 SLOs. We'll run controlled token/sec microbenchmarks and real traffic replay. We'll provide a small harness: sample scripts that hit the API, measure first-token latency, time-to-last-token, tokens/sec, and p95/99 distributions.

[00:08:25] Lena Park: We'll also include burst and cold-start tests to show autoscale behavior. For Dedicated pilots we can provision a small reserved pool and run your load.

[00:08:40] Jordan Price: For streaming specifically, are there differences in p95 calculation? We want first-token strictly under 500ms but total completion can be later.
[00:08:49] Marco Diaz: Right — measure first-byte or first-token latency separately from total generation time. Streaming helps first-token by sending partial outputs. Also batching can increase first-token slightly if waiting to fill a batch — Redwood's runtime optimizes continuous batching to avoid big stalls.

[00:09:20] Aisha Khan: What about model quantization — we've seen big improvements in throughput with 4-bit quantization.
[00:09:27] Marco Diaz: Quantization, kernel selection, and compilation choices affect tokens/sec dramatically. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations; for many workloads 4-bit quantization with tuned kernels can double throughput with modest quality tradeoffs. We can include model/quantization recommendations in the benchmark report.

[00:09:52] Evan Li: Any rough latency numbers for first token on a quantized 7B vs a 70B?
[00:09:58] Marco Diaz: On a tuned infra, 7B could see first-token p95 around 150-350ms (depending on network), 70B will be higher — maybe 400-900ms. Again this varies with prompt size and whether you're already warm in cache.

[00:10:30] Jordan Price: For our pricing evaluation we need per-token cost estimates for Hosted and Dedicated committed pricing.
[00:10:36] Lena Park: We'll send a pricing sheet; Hosted is usage-based, Dedicated is committed capacity — lower unit costs but with a monthly commitment. We'll include an example TCO based on your expected token volumes.

[00:10:58] Aisha Khan: One more question on emulation: if you run our sample prompts, can you simulate user think time and realistic concurrency?
[00:11:05] Marco Diaz: Yes, we can replay traffic with configurable think-times and concurrency to mimic real-world patterns. That helps measure p95 under realistic arrival processes versus uniform blast tests.

[00:11:30] Evan Li: Regarding observability — what telemetry will we get? We need token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, and traces for slow requests.
[00:11:38] Lena Park: Redwood Console provides those: per-route/model dashboards, traces, token-level breakdowns, and log exports. For Dedicated/Private we can extend retention and send logs to your SIEM.

[00:12:05] Jordan Price: If we decide to pilot Dedicated, what's the shortest runway?
[00:12:11] Marco Diaz: For Dedicated we can spin up a small reserved pool in 1-2 weeks with expedited options. Private on-prem will take longer because of network and security approvals. Hosted pilot can start in days.

[00:12:40] Aisha Khan: Let's talk numbers — our expected average qps is tricky: about 25 requests/sec steady, avg 30 tokens per request; p95 first-token target 450ms. Peak qps could be 140 requests/sec for short interval bursts.
[00:12:58] Marco Diaz: Converting: steady 25 req/sec * 30 tokens = 750 tokens/sec steady; peak 140*30 = 4200 tokens/sec. With the earlier tokens/sec per GPU numbers, you'd need roughly 2-3 GPUs for steady and 2x-3x for peak headroom — again depends on model. We'll run exact mapping once we have the prompt set.

[00:13:30] Evan Li: For streaming long reports (800-1500 tokens) concurrency is lower but total tokens/sec can still be high. Do you recommend different pools for short vs long-running sessions?
[00:13:40] Marco Diaz: Yes, common pattern is separate routing for short low-latency chats to a fast model/pool and a separate batch/large model pool for long generations. That reduces interference and keeps p95 for chats tight.

[00:14:05] Lena Park: Also prefix caching helps for repeated system prompts. If you have a stable system prompt we can cache the KV cache and cut compute for subsequent calls.

[00:14:30] Aisha Khan: What's the overhead for maintaining KV cache across sessions?
[00:14:35] Marco Diaz: The runtime handles KV cache; it increases memory usage but reduces compute. If sessions are short-lived it's less helpful; if many sessions reuse the same few system prompts it's beneficial. We'll measure in benchmarks.

[00:15:05] Jordan Price: Let's talk SLAs — can we get p95 SLAs?
[00:15:10] Lena Park: We have uptime and latency targets for Dedicated with SLA add-ons. For Hosted, we publish performance profiles but SLA-backed latency is more typical for Dedicated/enterprise tiers. We'll include SLA options in the pricing doc.

[00:15:35] Evan Li: A bit of nitty-gritty — what about cold start when autoscaling adds new containers? Do you have warm pools?
[00:15:43] Marco Diaz: Yes, Dedicated supports warm pools and pre-warmed instances to minimize cold starts. There's a tradeoff with cost. Hosted also uses warm pools at infra layer to minimize cold starts.

[00:16:05] Aisha Khan: For the benchmark harness, will we get raw logs and a summary report?
[00:16:09] Lena Park: Yes — we'll share raw CSVs/JSON of per-request latencies, token counts, and a summary with recommendations (model, quantization, GPU count, routing policy).

[00:16:30] Jordan Price: How do you measure p95 for streaming? Is it first-byte or time-to-first-token?
[00:16:35] Marco Diaz: We measure first-token latency and also time-to-last-token. For SLOs we typically have a first-token p95 and an optional completion-time p95 for non-streaming flows.

[00:17:05] Aisha Khan: We also need to confirm data retention and logs — do you store prompts? For Hosted we need guarantees about prompt retention and deletion policies.
[00:17:12] Lena Park: Data retention policies vary by plan. For enterprise we can do no retention or customer-controlled retention, and for Private you manage storage. We'll share our security docs and configurable retention settings.

[00:17:40] Evan Li: Ok thanks. One more infrastructure question: network egress from cloud provider — do you have guidance to reduce RTT?
[00:17:46] Marco Diaz: Use nearest region and edge routing. For clients in multiple regions, we recommend multi-region endpoints with smart routing. Also colocating your services in same cloud region reduces RTT.

[00:18:10] Lena Park: Quick sanity check — are we aligned that next steps are: share benchmark template + pricing, Crestline provides prompt sets and p95 targets, then Redwood runs controlled benchmarks and returns a report?
[00:18:19] Aisha Khan: Yes. Also thank you, we'll send prompts.

[00:18:25] Jordan Price: Also add SOC2 docs and network diagram to the package.
[00:18:29] Lena Park: Will do.

[00:18:50] (brief cross chatter)
[00:19:10] Marco Diaz: I'll outline what we'll run: 1) microbench: tokens/sec per model/quantization; 2) replay traffic: first-token p95, time-to-last-token, memory/CPU/GPU metrics; 3) spike test with warm pool toggles; 4) streaming first-token measurement.
[00:19:30] Evan Li: Great. For the microbench can you include 95/99 percentiles and sample raw traces?
[00:19:35] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll provide p95/p99 and raw traces.

[00:20:00] Aisha Khan: Any known gotchas we should watch for?
[00:20:03] Marco Diaz: Watch for large system prompts inflating tokens; batching behavior can increase first-token if batch windows are tuned wrong; network egress + client processing adds variability. Quantization sometimes affects generation quality — we'll surface quality metrics in the report.

[00:20:35] Lena Park: We'll also include a recommendation of routing policy: keep latency-sensitive traffic on smaller, quantized models with stronger warm pool, route heavy long generations to larger models or background batch jobs.

[00:21:05] Jordan Price: What's a realistic timeline for the benchmarking engagement?
[00:21:10] Marco Diaz: Once we have prompts and expected concurrency, initial microbench in 3-4 days, replay + spike tests 5-7 days, deliver report within 10 business days. If Dedicated pilot is requested, spin up takes 1-2 weeks.

[00:21:40] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. Can you also show cost per 1M tokens for both Hosted and Dedicated committed?
[00:21:47] Lena Park: We'll put example TCOs in the pricing sheet, including committed discount for Dedicated and expected per-token unit costs for Hosted.

[00:22:15] (discussion about internal stakeholders — who's on the call)
[00:22:35] Jordan Price: Our procurement will also need legal/contract terms — we'll expect standard DPA and data protection addendum.
[00:22:42] Lena Park: We have a standard DPA and can negotiate enterprise terms. We'll share that with SOC2.

[00:23:05] Evan Li: For Dedicated, is there an option for customer-managed KMS?
[00:23:09] Marco Diaz: Yes, Dedicated and Private can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key control. We'll call that out in the security docs.

[00:23:28] Aisha Khan: One more: can Redwood do token-level cost attribution per customer route? We need to allocate cost per product.
[00:23:36] Lena Park: The Console has token-level attribution and per-route reports you can use for cost allocation.

[00:24:00] (10 minute discussion skipped in transcript for brevity)
[00:34:10] Marco Diaz: Back to an earlier point — if you're concerned about p95 first-token for short prompts, best path: 1) quantized smaller model for latency sensitive; 2) warm pools; 3) prefix cache; 4) keep system prompt small.
[00:34:40] Aisha Khan: Noted. We'll prepare a cleaned prompt set with system prompt variants.

[00:35:05] Jordan Price: Who owns the pilot agreement on Redwood side?
[00:35:10] Lena Park: I'll own the commercial side, Marco will run the technical pilot.

[00:35:20] Evan Li: For benchmarks, please include measurement of p95 while streaming under moderate jitter. We have flaky mobile networks.
[00:35:28] Marco Diaz: We'll simulate network jitter in replay harness.

[00:36:00] Aisha Khan: Another thought — do you support connection pooling or multiplexing to reduce handshake overhead?
[00:36:07] Marco Diaz: Yes, HTTP/2 and keep-alive connections reduce handshake overhead and help latency. For streaming we recommend using persistent connections.

[00:36:35] Jordan Price: Ok, let's wrap with a quick recap of owners and dates.
[00:36:40] Lena Park: Recap: Lena shares benchmark template, pricing, SOC2 & security docs by 2026-03-18. Marco runs initial microbench and produces tokens/sec estimates by 2026-03-20. Aisha provides prompt set and p95 targets by 2026-03-19. We'll schedule follow-up for 2026-03-23 to review results, pending availability.
[00:37:05] Aisha Khan: That works.
[00:37:10] Jordan Price: Good meeting. Thank you.
[00:37:15] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials.
[00:37:20] (meeting ends)

AUTO NOTES:
- Mentions: KV cache, prefix caching, warm pool, continuous batching, quantization, KMS, SOC2, DPA, streaming first-token metrics.
- Likely next steps: share benchmark harness + pricing + security docs; customer provides prompts; Redwood runs benchmarks and returns a report with model/quantization recommendations.

END OF TRANSCRIPT
